idiom_name: for-range over the decoded parts + per-part Send
implementation_notes: The smallest complete Go splitter is a for-range over the decoded slice with one publish per element: there is no role structure to replace, and the messaging client (Kafka, NATS, AMQP) only needs a per-part Send. Concurrency is added with goroutines plus a channel and an errgroup rather than with a Splitter object, and correlation/sequence headers are set explicitly on every part because nothing in the runtime fills them in. A splitter type is justified only when the boundary rule itself must be pluggable (a map from payload kind to a split function).
pitfalls: Before Go 1.22 the loop variable was shared across iterations: a goroutine per part captured the last element unless the value was copied or passed as an argument.
Publishing without honouring ctx or back-pressure turns a slow broker into unbounded memory growth.
A single shared error variable (or an ignored Send error) reports success after a partial publication; collect per-part errors and decide whether the composite failed.
Sequence metadata must come from the composite, not from a package-level counter shared by concurrent splits.

variants.name: Range-over-func iterator (slices.Chunk + iter.Seq)
variants.idiom_name: slices.Chunk / iter.Seq as a composed split stage
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.23's range-over-func plus the iter package make the splitter an iterator: slices.Chunk returns an iterator over consecutive sub-slices of up to n elements, and a hand-written iter.Seq can lazily yield one part per element, so the split becomes a composable stage that the consumer ranges over instead of a loop that owns the fan-out. This is the idiomatic Go analogue of a stream operator and the right shape when several stages (decode, chunk, publish) should stay separate; the plain loop stays simpler for a one-off split.
pitfalls: slices.Chunk yields sub-slices that alias the original backing array: mutating a part mutates the composite, and concurrent consumers then race on shared memory.
An iterator is a stateful single-use value - ranging the same iter.Seq twice publishes nothing the second time unless it is rebuilt.
A yield function that is not called on every element (early return without draining) can leak the producer goroutine when the iterator is channel-backed.
